title: What Are Public and Private Keys?
plain:
Bitcoin does not check names or passwords. A matched pair of keys decides who owns what.

A private key is a secret number that proves you own certain bitcoin and lets you spend it. Its partner, the public key, is safe to share: other people use it to send you bitcoin. Together they are called a key pair.

When you spend bitcoin, your wallet — the app or device that manages your keys — uses your private key to make a digital signature. A digital signature is a piece of mathematical proof that only your private key can produce. Anyone on the Bitcoin network (the computers that keep it running) can check that it is genuine using your public key. Only you can produce it, like a handwritten signature.

You almost never see your private keys. Your wallet creates them. It starts from a seed, a random master number made by a secure random number generator. From that one seed it can create all the keys you will ever need. That is why backing up a single seed phrase — the list of words that represents the seed — protects every key your wallet makes.

A surprise for many people: a wallet does not hold actual bitcoin. It holds only the keys. The bitcoin itself is recorded on the blockchain, Bitcoin's shared public ledger, much like a bank balance is really a number in the bank's database.

Private keys are very large numbers. Even so, guessing a valid one is far harder than guessing a bank card number and its PIN together.

The hard part: if you lose your private keys and have no seed phrase backup, that bitcoin is gone for good. For large amounts, keep your keys in cold storage — a hardware wallet, meaning a small device that holds your private keys offline, such as a Ledger Nano S or a Trezor One — rather than a hot wallet, an internet-connected app. With cold storage you alone are responsible: no company can rescue you if you lose the device or the backup. That responsibility is called self-custody.
technical:
Bitcoin uses public-key cryptography: a wallet generates a key pair consisting of a private key and a corresponding public key. The public key receives bitcoin; the private key produces the digital signature required to spend it. A signature can only be computed with the private key, but anyone on the network can verify it with the public key alone, making the private key an unforgeable identity: spending authority is bound to key control, not to a person or account record.

Key generation is normally invisible to the user. The wallet uses an industry-standard derivation scheme (the source does not name it; in practice this is BIP-32/BIP-39 hierarchical deterministic wallets): a secure random number generator produces a seed, from which the wallet derives as many private keys as needed. Consequently only the seed — backed up as a seed phrase — must be stored, not each individual key.

Wallets hold keys, not bitcoin. Ownership is recorded on the blockchain, analogous to a bank storing checking-account balances in its database. In the source's example, Bob's wallet signs a transaction paying Alice's public key with Bob's private key; the network validates the signature against the public key, and the funds become spendable by whoever controls the corresponding private key.

Private keys are very large numbers; the source asserts, without figures, that guessing a valid one is far harder than guessing a credit card number plus PIN.

Storage: for large amounts, cold storage is recommended — typically a hardware wallet such as a Ledger Nano S or Trezor One. Hot wallets are internet-connected web or mobile apps chosen for convenience. Self-custody means no third-party recourse if the device or seed phrase is lost; the optimal choice varies by user.

claims.claim: In Bitcoin, a private key proves ownership of the funds corresponding to a given address and is used to create the signatures required to spend bitcoin.
Bitcoin uses public key cryptography to create a key pair: the public key is used to receive bitcoin, while the private key signs transactions to spend it.
When a public key and signature are presented, anyone on the Bitcoin network can verify the transaction as valid, confirming the spender is the true owner of the funds.
Private keys are usually generated by the user's Bitcoin wallet, and users almost never see or directly interact with them.
claims.source: Section 'How is a private key generated?'.

claims.claim: Wallets use a secure random number generator to generate a seed, from which as many private keys as needed can be derived; only one seed must be backed up rather than each unique private key.
claims.source: Section 'How is a private key generated?'.

claims.claim: A digital signature can only be created using the private key, but its validity can be verified using only the public key, allowing a private key to serve as an unforgeable identity.
Bitcoin wallets do not hold actual bitcoin; they hold only the keys. Bitcoin is stored on the blockchain, similarly to how a checking account is stored in a bank's database.
claims.source: Callout note in 'How private keys are used in a transaction'.

claims.claim: If a user loses their private keys and does not have the wallet's seed phrase, they lose access to any funds associated with those private keys.
claims.source: Section 'How do I store my bitcoin private key?'.

claims.claim: Anyone who knows a private key controls all bitcoin under that key; ownership of bitcoin is directly based on control of private keys.
Private keys are very large numbers, but guessing a valid one is far more difficult than guessing a credit card and PIN number.
For storing large amounts of bitcoin, a cold storage wallet is considered best; for most users this takes the form of a hardware wallet such as a Ledger Nano S or a Trezor One.
Hot wallets are internet-connected software applications, typically web or mobile apps, that store a user's private keys for convenient, fast access.

With cold storage, the user is responsible for key security with no recourse to a third party if the device or seed phrase is lost; this is known as self-custody, and the most secure solution varies by user.

warnings: Anyone who knows your private key (or your seed phrase) controls all the bitcoin under that key — never share it with anyone you would not trust with all of your money.
If you lose your private keys and have no seed phrase backup, that bitcoin is gone permanently — no bank, company, or Bitcoin service can restore it.
For large amounts of bitcoin, keep your keys in cold storage (an offline hardware wallet), not an internet-connected hot wallet.

notes_for_reviewer: 1) The source's Bob-and-Alice example has Bob entering Alice's 'public key' as the recipient; in practice Bitcoin payments go to addresses derived from public keys. I preserved the source's simplification but the plain text avoids restating it — consider adding an address-vs-public-key distinction for advanced readers. 2) The source says wallets use 'an industry standard to derive private keys' without naming it; the technical text identifies this as BIP-32/39 HD wallets — verify this addition. 3) The provided source text contains no URL; the river.com/learn URL is inferred from River's article-title pattern and must be confirmed before publishing. 4) Ledger Nano S and Trezor One are older hardware wallet models (the Nano S has been discontinued by the manufacturer); check staleness before endorsing specific devices. 5) The credit-card-plus-PIN guessing comparison is qualitative; the source gives no entropy figures. 6) Risk class set to caution, not danger, because the source contains no procedural reset/delete/reseed instructions — only warnings about key loss and custody trade-offs. 7) The seed phrase word count (commonly 12 or 24 words) is not stated in the source and was deliberately omitted.
